result: The manuscript provides background on TP53 as a tumor suppressor, noting it is mutated in >50% of human tumors, that Li-Fraumeni patients with germline mutations are cancer-prone, and that TP53 can be inactivated by point mutations (creating dominant-negative proteins) or deletions, with different transcriptional consequences.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C14, C15, C16, C17, and C18 are well-established facts in the TP53 literature and are appropriately cited. These background claims provide context for the study and are supported by the referenced literature.

result: The manuscript reviews prior mouse models of Tp53 deficiency, noting that both mutant and null alleles cause cancer, but with different tumor spectra depending on the specific allele. Li-Fraumeni patients can harbor TP53 deletions, and cancers in heterozygous carriers often lose the second allele.
evaluation: Claims C19–C26 accurately summarize the mouse Tp53 literature and human Li-Fraumeni syndrome, with appropriate citations. These are well-established findings that provide rationale for the current study.

result: The manuscript reviews TP53's role in sarcomas, particularly ERMS, noting that TP53 is mutated in 16% of ERMS, that TP53 pathway disruption occurs in >30% of ERMS, that mutations are acquired at relapse, and that Li-Fraumeni patients develop ERMS. Existing mouse and xenograft ERMS models do not metastasize, and no syngeneic zebrafish tp53 deletion models existed prior to this work.
evaluation: Claims C27–C34 accurately cite the ERMS literature and identify gaps in existing models that motivate the current study. The claims about limitations of existing models (C33, C34) are appropriately stated as knowledge claims.

result: The authors generated a tp53 deletion zebrafish model using TALENs in the syngeneic CG1 strain, deleting 12.1 kb encompassing the entire tp53 coding sequence. Homozygous mutants lack Tp53 protein, are resistant to radiation-induced apoptosis, and survive to adulthood at expected Mendelian ratios.
evaluation: Claims C35, C40–C43, C101–C104 are supported by the methods description, Figure 1A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1. Western blot confirms protein loss (C41), TUNEL assay confirms apoptosis resistance (C42, p<0.001), and survival data confirm viability (C43). The model generation is well-documented.

result: tp53del/del zebrafish spontaneously develop a wide tumor spectrum including leukemia (starting at 4 months), MPNSTs, angiosarcomas, and germ cell tumors. By 12 months, 37% developed externally visible tumors. The spectrum is wider than in tp53 point-mutant zebrafish and more similar to Tp53-null mice, though T cell lymphomas (predominant in mice) were not observed.
evaluation: Claims C3–C6, C44–C47, C51–C56 are supported by histopathology (Figure 1B–M), tumor incidence data (Figure 1N), and tumor spectrum quantification (Figure 1O). The comparison to point-mutant zebrafish (C52, C53) and Tp53-null mice (C54) is appropriately cited. The interpretation of species differences (C55, C56) is reasonable speculation based on the data.

result: The authors claim that no animal model of aggressive NK cell-like leukemia (ANKL) existed prior to this study.
evaluation: Claims C7 and C85 state that no animal model of ANKL has been developed. While this may be accurate based on the authors' literature review, comprehensive verification of the absence of any such model worldwide is difficult. The claim is plausible but cannot be definitively confirmed without exhaustive literature review.

result: MPNST diagnosis was validated by sox10 immunohistochemistry, a well-established clinical marker. Heterozygous tp53wt/del zebrafish infrequently developed tumors, consistent with mouse models.
evaluation: Claims C48–C50 are supported by Figure 1J showing sox10 IHC and appropriate citation (Shin et al., 2012). The low tumor incidence in heterozygotes (C50) is consistent with cited mouse models and expected for a recessive tumor suppressor phenotype.

result: tp53del/del tumors (MPNSTs, angiosarcomas, leukemias, and ERMS) efficiently transplanted into syngeneic CG1 recipients with high engraftment rates (9/9 MPNSTs, 8/9 angiosarcomas, 25/25 leukemias, 47/49 ERMS). GFP-labeled tumors were traceable, leukemia cells invaded kidney marrow (up to 45% of marrow), and histology was similar between primary and transplanted tumors.
evaluation: Claims C57–C64, C67, C68, C37 are well-supported by Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, showing whole animal imaging, histology, and flow cytometry. Engraftment rates are clearly documented and high across all tumor types, demonstrating the utility of the syngeneic model.

result: Leukemia cells displayed morphology consistent with aggressive NK cell leukemia (large cells with prominent nucleoli and vacuolated cytoplasm). Gene expression profiling classified these as NK cell-like leukemias, expressing NK markers (il2ga/b, jak3, perforins) but lacking other hematopoietic lineage markers. The top 200 leukemia genes were significantly enriched only in NK cells (p=0.015).
evaluation: Claims C65–C66, C77–C80 are supported by cytospin/Wright-Giemsa staining (Figure 2O–R), RNA-seq analysis (Figure 3D–E), and statistical testing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, p=0.015). The NK cell classification is based on multiple independent lines of evidence including morphology, gene expression signatures, and lineage-specific marker expression.

result: The manuscript reviews human ANKL, noting poor prognosis, perforin expression, lack of T/B cell markers, association with EBV (though EBV-negative cases exist), and that TP53 mutations/deletions have been identified in human ANKL.
evaluation: Claims C81–C84 accurately cite the human ANKL literature (Liang and Graham, 2008; Suzuki and Nakamura, 1999; Soliman et al., 2014; Yagita et al., 2000). These provide important context linking the zebrafish model to human disease.

result: RNA-seq and principal component analysis identified six distinct tumor clusters. Each tumor type showed enrichment for GO terms consistent with predicted cell of origin: leukemias (immune processes), angiosarcomas (vasculature/blood vessel morphogenesis), germ cell tumors (sexual reproduction/gamete formation), and ERMS (muscle structure/contraction/development). Zebrafish tumors shared gene expression signatures with corresponding human tumors.
evaluation: Claims C69–C73, C10 are supported by Figure 3A (PCA), Figure 3B (heatmap), Figure 3C (GO enrichment), and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C (GSEA showing significant enrichment of human tumor signatures in corresponding zebrafish tumors with FDR q-values ≤0.004). The transcriptional profiling provides strong evidence for cell-of-origin identity and human disease relevance.

result: GSEA analysis showed significant enrichment of human tumor signatures in corresponding zebrafish tumors: angiosarcoma (FDR q=0.001), MPNST (FDR q=0.004), and ERMS (FDR q=0).
evaluation: Claims C74–C76 are directly supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C showing GSEA enrichment plots with reported FDR q-values. The statistical significance is strong, particularly for ERMS (q=0).

result: Comparison of tp53del/del and tp53M214K/M214K MPNSTs showed significant overlap in gene expression (p=4e-321 for up-regulated, p=5e-182 for down-regulated genes), confirming loss-of-function activity of tp53M214K. However, differences in expression were also noted, likely reflecting distinct effects of deletion versus point mutation.
evaluation: Claims C86–C88 are supported by RNA-seq comparison with statistical analysis (Fisher's exact test). The significant overlap (C86) confirms tp53M214K is loss-of-function (C87), while observed differences (C88) are reasonably attributed to mutation type, consistent with mouse model literature.

result: Despite TP53's known roles in regulating stem cell self-renewal in other cancers, limiting dilution transplantation assays showed that tp53 loss did not alter the frequency of tumor-propagating stem cells in ERMS (p=0.647). The authors conclude that Tp53 loss-of-function does not affect cancer stem cell frequency in ERMS.
evaluation: Claims C89–C91, C38, C12 are supported by Table 1 showing limiting dilution data with ELDA analysis (p=0.647, not significant). The experimental design is appropriate, sample sizes are adequate (n≥3 tumors per genotype), and the statistical analysis is correct. The conclusion that tp53 loss does not affect stem cell frequency is justified by the data.

result: The manuscript cites prior work showing that NOTCH1, MYF5/MYOD, and WNT signaling regulate self-renewal and tumor-sustaining cell numbers in rhabdomyosarcoma.
evaluation: Claim C92 appropriately cites relevant literature (Chen et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2018; Ignatius et al., 2017; Tenente et al., 2017) to contrast with the current finding that tp53 does not affect stem cell frequency.

result: tp53del/del ERMS showed significantly increased invasion and metastasis compared to tp53wt/wt ERMS (28/102 vs 5/58 fish with metastases, p=0.003). Metastatic lesions were confirmed by histology and GFP IHC. The authors conclude that tp53 loss stimulates invasion/metastasis in ERMS, potentially explaining poor outcomes in human ERMS with TP53 pathway disruption.
evaluation: Claims C93–C98, C11, C39 are supported by Figure 4 showing serial imaging, quantification (p=0.003, Fisher's exact test), and histological confirmation (Figure 4G–H). The experimental design is appropriate with adequate sample sizes (n=5 tp53wt/wt tumors, n=11 tp53del/del tumors, 7–15 recipients per tumor). The statistical significance is strong and the conclusion about pro-metastatic effects is justified.

result: The authors suggest that TP53 loss-of-function has novel pro-metastatic roles in human muscle tumors and that TP53 has a likely role in ERMS progression and therapy resistance.
evaluation: Claims C13 and C31 are reasonable inferences from the experimental data showing increased metastasis without changes in stem cell frequency (C11, C12, C95) and from cited literature on TP53 mutations at ERMS relapse (C30). The inference is logical and supported by the data, though direct human validation would strengthen the claim.

result: The authors claim that unlike mouse models and human xenografts, zebrafish ERMS are metastatic and can be readily quantified and visualized in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C99–C100 are supported by the metastasis data in Figure 4 and the statement in C33 that existing mouse/xenograft models do not metastasize. The zebrafish model's ability to visualize and quantify metastasis is clearly demonstrated by serial GFP imaging and statistical analysis.

result: The tp53del/del model contrasts with tp53 point-mutation zebrafish models that predominantly develop MPNSTs.
evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by comparison of tumor spectra (Figure 1O) and citation to Berghmans et al., 2005 (C53). The deletion model shows a wider spectrum including substantial leukemia and angiosarcoma, unlike point-mutant models.
